what.question: What is Incremental, exactly?
what.answer: An infrastructure layer for enterprise AI. It connects your data and systems, runs agents and workflows against them, and records what happened.

replace.question: Do we have to replace our stack?
replace.answer: No. Incremental reads from the systems and the warehouse you already run. Connecting a single source is enough to start.

trust.question: How do we know what an agent did?
trust.answer: Every run keeps its inputs, tool calls, and outputs, attributed to an identity and exportable for audit.

start.question: What does getting started look like?

intro.title: Software that understands your business
intro.lead: Most AI tooling stops at the model. The hard part is everything around it: the data it reads, the systems it touches, the permissions it inherits, and the record of what it did.

body.a: Incremental is the layer that handles the rest. Connect the systems you already run, define the entities your business actually uses, and build agents and workflows that act on them under the same rules your people follow.
body.b: Nothing is a black box. Every run keeps its inputs, its decisions, and its outputs, so what happens in production stays something you can inspect, explain, and improve.

how.title: How a benchmark run works
how.description: Public tasks, a fixed harness, and a transcript for every attempt, so a result can be checked rather than believed.

capabilities.title: What makes a number trustworthy

faq.title: Before you cite a result

cadence.content: Re-run each quarter, with a rotating held-out set and a versioned harness.

why.question: Why another benchmark?
why.answer: Existing sets measure reasoning on puzzles. Almost none measure whether a system can finish a piece of ordinary business work.

gaming.question: What stops a system training on it?
gaming.answer: Part of the set is held out and rotated each cycle, and results are reported separately for the public and held-out halves.

submit.question: Can we submit our own system?

compare.question: How should we read the numbers?
compare.answer: As a ranking on this task set, not a general claim. Read a few transcripts before you trust a gap.

a.label: Certification and enablement
a.content: Your engineers train on the same material our own solutions team uses. Certification is per person and free, and it is what unlocks joint delivery and the partner directory listing.

b.label: Commercial terms
b.content: Margin on resold consumption, referral fees on sourced deals, and no minimum commitment in the first year. Terms are the same for every partner at a given tier and published, not negotiated case by case.

c.label: Support during delivery
c.content: A named contact for every active engagement, escalation into the engineering team for platform issues, and shared architecture review before anything goes to production.

d.label: What we ask
d.content: Two certified engineers to reach the first tier, a reference deployment within six months, and a named partner lead we can reach when a customer escalates.

a.question: How long does the application take?
a.answer: Most firms hear back within a week and complete certification inside a month. The gate is your engineers finishing the training, not our review.

b.question: Do we need existing AI expertise?
b.answer: No. The firms that do best already know how to deliver enterprise software into a regulated environment. The platform specifics are what the certification covers.

c.question: Can we partner on more than one track?
c.answer: Yes, and many firms do. Delivery and advisory in particular tend to sit in the same practice, and the certification counts once.

d.question: Who owns the customer relationship?
d.answer: You do, on engagements you source. On deals we refer, the contract structure is agreed before the introduction rather than after.

a.label: Certified engineers on your account
a.content: Ask how many people assigned to your engagement hold current certification, not how many the firm employs in total.

b.label: Reference deployments in your sector
b.content: A partner who has already worked inside your regulatory constraints will spend the first month building rather than learning them.

c.label: A named handover plan
c.content: Agree upfront who operates the deployment after launch. A partner who cannot describe the handover is planning to stay indefinitely.

d.label: Ownership of what gets built
d.content: Workflows, connectors, and policies built during the engagement should be yours. Confirm it in the statement of work rather than assuming it.

a.question: Do we need a partner at all?
a.answer: Not always. Teams with in house engineers often ship the first workflow themselves. Partners earn their place on scope, regulated environments, and speed.

b.question: How are partners vetted?
b.answer: Every listed firm holds current certification, has shipped a reference deployment, and carries a named lead we can reach when something escalates.

c.question: What does an engagement typically cost?
c.answer: Partners set their own rates. A scoping engagement is usually a few weeks; ask for a fixed price on that stage before committing to the build.

d.question: Can we switch partners later?
d.answer: Yes. What gets built belongs to you and runs on your own deployment, so moving to another firm or in house does not mean rebuilding.
